title: Area and the distributive property
keyIdea: Cut a rectangle into two parts and no tiles are lost. A rectangle 3 tall and 4 + 2 long has area 3 × 6 = 18, and its parts have 3 × 4 = 12 and 3 × 2 = 6, so 3 × (4 + 2) = 3 × 4 + 3 × 2. This is the distributive property. It turns a hard times fact into two easy ones: 6 × 13 = 6 × 10 + 6 × 3 = 60 + 18 = 78. Both parts share the same height, so the number outside the brackets multiplies each part.
familyTip: Use a bar of chocolate, a tray of ice cubes or squared paper. Snap or draw a line across it and ask: how many squares in each part, and in all? Then try a shopping sum like 4 packs of 12: 4 × 10 is 40, 4 × 2 is 8, so 48.

visual.caption: Does each sum give the same area as 4 × 13? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: tile a 3 by 6 rectangle, cut it without losing a tile, try every cut, split 6 × 13 at ten, and build area models for bracket equations.

kid: Area is how many squares cover a shape. A rectangle 3 squares tall and 6 long has 3 rows of 6. That is 3 × 6 = 18 squares.
Now cut it with one straight line from top to bottom. One part is 3 by 4. The other part is 3 by 2. That gives 12 squares and 6 squares. 12 + 6 = 18. No square went away.
So 3 × 6 is the same as 3 × 4 + 3 × 2. We write it as 3 × (4 + 2) = 3 × 4 + 3 × 2. The 3 is the height. Both parts have it, so both parts get times 3.
This helps with big facts. For 6 × 13, cut 13 into 10 and 3. Then 6 × 10 = 60 and 6 × 3 = 18. Add them: 60 + 18 = 78. Do not forget to times the small part too.
adult: Ages 8 to 9. This is US Common Core 3.MD.C.7c, use tiling to show that the area of a rectangle with whole-number sides a and b + c is the sum of a × b and a × c, and 3.OA.B.5, apply the distributive property. It supports partitioning in Year 3 and Year 4 multiplication in the National Curriculum in England. Key words: area, square unit, tiling, area model, partition, distributive property, brackets.

The area model is the bridge from counting tiles to written multiplication. A rectangle split into two parts shows why each part must be multiplied by the shared side. Later the same picture explains the grid method, long multiplication and expanding brackets such as 3(x + 2) = 3x + 6.

Common mistakes: multiplying only the first part, so 6 × 13 becomes 6 × 10 + 3 = 63; adding the sides instead of multiplying them, so a 3 by 6 rectangle seems to be 9; thinking a cut loses some area; multiplying the two parts together instead of adding them; and using a number inside the brackets as the shared side.

In the lab your child lays columns of tiles over a 3 by 6 rectangle, then drags a cut line and sees 3 × 4 + 3 × 2 stay at 18. They try three cuts, split 6 × 13 at ten to get 60 + 18, see why 6 × 10 + 3 leaves out 15 tiles, and build area models for three bracket equations.

practice.prompt: A rectangle is {r} squares tall and {a} + {b} squares long. What is its area in square units?
practice.hint: Find {r} × {a} and {r} × {b}, then add the two parts.
Both parts of the rectangle are 5 tall. Multiply each part by 5.
Cut 1{b} into 10 and {b}. Work out {r} × 10 and {r} × {b}.

practice.prompt: A 4 by 9 rectangle is cut into a 4 by 5 part and a 4 by 4 part. What is the total area?
choices: Less than 36, because of the cut
practice.hint: Find the area of each part. A cut does not lose any squares.
The number outside the brackets is the side both parts share.
practice.explain: Both parts are 3 tall. The widths are 6 and 4, so the whole is 3 by 10.

Both parts are {r} tall. Put the two widths together.
pool.explain: The widths {a} and {b} join to make {=a+b}, so it is {r} × {=a+b}.

pool.prompt: Mia works out 7 × 12 as 7 × 10 + 2 = 72. What went wrong?
choices: She did not multiply the 2 by 7
pool.hint: Draw it: the small part is 7 tall and 2 wide.
pool.explain: The small part is 7 × 2 = 14, not 2. So 7 × 12 = 70 + 14 = 84.

pool.prompt: Which sum gives the area of a 6 by 15 rectangle?
pool.hint: Cut 15 into 10 and 5. The two parts sit side by side, so add them.

pool.prompt: A garden is {r} m wide. It has a {a} m long lawn and a {b} m long patio side by side. What is the total area in square metres?
pool.hint: Find the lawn area and the patio area. Then add.

pool.prompt: A 5 by 8 rectangle is cut into two parts. One part is 5 by 3. What is the other part?
pool.hint: The cut runs top to bottom, so the height stays 5. What is left of 8?
pool.explain: 8 − 3 = 5, so the other part is 5 by 5. 15 + 25 = 40 = 5 × 8.

pool.prompt: Which is easiest for working out 8 × 14 in your head?
pool.hint: All three are correct. Which has a part that is times 10?
pool.explain: 8 × 10 = 80 is quick, and 8 × 4 = 32. So 8 × 14 = 112. The other cuts work too, but are harder.

pool.prompt: Tom says a 4 by 7 rectangle has area 11. What did he do?
choices: He added the sides instead of multiplying
pool.hint: Is 4 + 7 or 4 × 7 the number of squares?
pool.explain: 4 + 7 = 11 adds the sides. There are 4 rows of 7 squares, so the area is 4 × 7 = 28.
